analysis.file_name: Q3 GDP underscores Warsh's go-slow approach, we will see in Dec how serious Warsh really is. .pdf
analysis.title: Q3 GDP underscores Warsh's go-slow approach, we will see in Dec how serious Warsh really is
key_insights: Net drivers of Q3 real GDP growth were discretionary spending by consumers and the Federal government. Real GDP rose $200bn in Q3. Discretionary real consumption rose $86bn and defense spending rose $25bn, together 54% of the GDP increase and an average of 58% in 2026 YTD.

Combined inventories, nonpetroleum goods imports, and business spending on equipment and intellectual property fell by $5bn in Q3. Surging AI equipment spending is being offset by imports, and construction spending has yet to affect overall GDP.

Consumption upside for discretionary items looks limited by the higher cost of necessities. Federal spending has no upside limit, and a 'blue wave' would swap defense allocations into transfers without slowing the overall pace of spending.

Warsh sees the current rate increases as a mini version of 2022-23: moving policy rates to where inflation is likely to settle as tariffs roll off and the war with Iran ends, rather than where inflation is now. He plans one more hike and then cuts in 2027.
A funds rate set to the current pace of inflation would be 100bp higher, assuming a neutral rate of 1%.

TS Lombard sees a higher rate path being forced on Warsh. Nominal growth in final sales of domestic product averages about 6%, against non-financial CP A2/P2 at 4.3% and the 10Y UST at 5%. Bank lending is growing at a 7.4% SAAR as of mid-October, reaccelerating since mid-July.
Financial conditions are described as far from tight. The AI sector revaluation of equity prices and borrowing spreads is viewed as markets functioning, not distress.
Higher commodity prices are expected to pass through to goods prices excluding food and energy, then to services prices with a lag. Federal deficit growth offsets the impact of monetary tightening.
TS Lombard expects at least a 100bp funds rate increase over the next 12 months, or sooner if Warsh is as serious as he says.
Market-implied probability of a 50bp hike in December is zero. The author considers taking the other side a reasonable bet and expects Warsh to hike more than he or the market expects.

The 10Y yield is rallying on pressured-consumer worries, probably to 5.70%-5.75% according to the author. Coming data on inflation, employment and spending will decide how serious Warsh is in December.

Defense and consumption together are 54% of the Q3 GDP increase.

risk_factors: Sep consumer spending drop offset the Aug surge, so the monthly data are noisy
Data over coming weeks may show weaker inflation, employment or spending, which would undermine the hike case
Consumers are pressured, which is driving the current bond rally
AI sector revaluation of equity prices and borrowing spreads
Author notes there are numerous alternative outcomes to the outlook
vol_and_positioning: Market pricing assigns zero probability to a 50bp hike at the December FOMC, which the author calls an invitation to take the other side.
geopolitical: War with Iran, which Warsh expects to end
Tariffs expected to roll off, per Warsh's inflation view
Possible 'blue wave' in elections, expected to shift defense allocations into transfers

tension_points.bull_case: Warsh sees the current hikes as a mini 2022-23 cycle: one more hike then cuts in 2027, as tariffs roll off, the Iran war ends, and AI-related income destruction among higher-skilled workers weighs on spending.
tension_points.bear_case: TS Lombard argues nominal growth near 6%, accelerating bank lending, loose financial conditions, commodity pass-through and deficit spending will force at least 100bp of hikes over 12 months.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Data over the coming weeks failing to show sustained inflation, employment and resumed spending would weaken the hike case.
